scenario.context: The Golden Tankard tavern is famous for its signature ale, which the owner, Bram, claims is so pure it never gives drinkers a hangover.
scenario.text: "My ale is brewed with crystal-clear spring water, so no one ever gets a hangover. If you did feel lousy this morning, you must have mixed it with some cheap spirit or eaten too much fried food. The brew itself is flawless!"
scenario.speaker_context: Bram the tavern owner constantly adds new excuses—bad food, lack of sleep, personal weakness—whenever a patron reports a hangover after drinking his ale.

structure.pattern_description: When a claim is shown to be false, the speaker moves the goalposts by adding ad‑hoc exceptions so the claim can never be falsified.
structure.formal_form: P asserts X. Evidence shows X is false. P revises X to X' by appending exception E, rendering the counter‑evidence irrelevant.
structure.why_wrong: Each new exception shields the original claim from any possible refutation, making the claim unfalsifiable. An unfalsifiable claim cannot be meaningfully supported or disproved, indicating faulty reasoning.
structure.counterpoint: Under what exact conditions would you admit your ale can cause a hangover? If every failure is blamed on something else, the claim that the ale never causes hangovers is meaningless.

assessment.identification_prompt: Each time a patron complains of a hangover, Bram adds a new excuse. What logical error is he committing?

rubric.description: Accepts Bram's excuses without question, perhaps believing the hangover was caused by the patron.
Notes that something seems off but treats each individual excuse as plausible.
Recognizes a pattern of new excuses but cannot name the specific fallacy.
Identifies the error as special pleading (no true Scotsman) and explains how moving the goalposts protects the claim.
Names the fallacy, describes the unfalsifiability problem, and can articulate how to challenge Bram’s reasoning.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: Notice how the claim changes each time a counter‑example appears. What new condition does Bram add to keep his original statement safe?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! You spotted the special pleading. Explain to Bram that without a fixed standard his claim can never be tested.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boisterous, proud of his brew, defensive when his reputation is challenged, quick to offer ad‑hoc explanations.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "My ale never gives anyone a hangover—unless you..."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present a series of independent hangover reports. Bram will respond with new excuses. The player must identify the special pleading pattern; once identified, Bram may agree to a blind taste‑test without his usual justifications, leading to a quest to improve the tavern's reputation.

scenario.context: In the Grand Library Archive, Senior Archivist Marwen is addressing the Council of Scholars. He wants the council to approve the removal of several centuries‑old parchment collections to make room for a new digitalization wing.
scenario.text: Everyone knows that outdated documents only clutter our halls—this is simply beyond dispute. Moreover, most preservation experts agree that digitizing is the future, so we can safely discard the physical copies. Granted, some historians value the originals, but the benefits of a modern archive outweigh sentimental attachment.
scenario.speaker_context: Archivist Marwen uses three rhetorical moves: an assuring claim that suppresses doubt, a guarding appeal to authority, and a discounting concession that acknowledges but then dismisses objections.

structure.pattern_description: Three coordinated rhetorical moves that manage acceptance: assuring ('Everyone knows…') discourages questioning, guarding ('Most experts agree…') hedges while sounding authoritative, discounting ('Granted …, but…') acknowledges a counterpoint then dismisses it.
structure.formal_form: Assuring: 'Everyone knows P' (implies questioning P is unreasonable). Guarding: 'Most experts say Q' (offers a vague authority). Discounting: 'Granted R, but S' (recognizes R but dismisses it in favor of S).
structure.why_wrong: The moves replace actual evidence with social pressure and unnamed authority. 'Everyone knows' offers no data, 'most experts' is cited without any specific source, and the 'granted but' clause acknowledges a real concern without genuinely weighing it against the proposed benefit.
structure.why_right: When used honestly, these moves can be legitimate. An assuring statement can reference widely accepted facts, guarding can cite genuine expert consensus, and discounting can fairly address a minor objection after proper analysis.
structure.counterpoint: Demand specifics: Who exactly knows this? Which preservation experts endorse digitization, and can you provide their studies? You 'granted' historians' attachment—how does the benefit quantitatively outweigh the loss of the originals?

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify the assuring, guarding, and discounting moves in Marwen's speech and judge whether each is being used legitimately or as a logical shortcut.

rubric.description: Accepts the speech wholesale, sees no problem, and cannot name any of the three moves.
Names at most one move correctly but treats it as entirely legitimate without critique.
Identifies two moves correctly and notes a possible issue, but does not evaluate all three.
Correctly identifies all three moves and provides a basic justification for why each may be illegitimate.
Accurately labels all three moves, explains the logical weakness of each, and proposes concrete evidence or questions that would expose the shortcut.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Prompt the learner to ask the archivist: "Which scholars specifically support digitization, and can you share the studies?" Encourage them to request concrete data before accepting the claim.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the analysis and ask the learner to suggest an alternative solution that respects the originals while still modernizing the archive.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Meticulous yet persuasive; values efficiency but enjoys rhetorical flair.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: I propose we clear the old shelves to make way for a state‑of‑the‑art digital hub. The old scrolls are more hindrance than help.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) demand citations and postpone the decision, (b) suggest a hybrid approach—digitize and store originals in climate‑controlled vaults, or (c) accept the proposal and gain a modest reputation boost with the archivist.

scenario.context: Captain Aria steps into the Navigator's Log Cabin aboard the merchant vessel *Sea‑Hawk*. Two ancient log entries are etched on brass plates. The ship's seasoned first mate, Joren, challenges her to test the arguments.
scenario.text:
Log Entry Alpha reads: 
1. Every vessel that carries gold must have a reinforced hull. 
2. The *Sea‑Hawk* carries gold. 
3. Therefore, the *Sea‑Hawk* has a reinforced hull.

Log Entry Beta reads: 
1. Captain Aria commanded the *Sea‑Hawk* during the storm of the Crimson Reef. 
2. Therefore, Captain Aria is an experienced sailor.

Joren says: "One of these arguments is valid, the other is not. Both have issues. Identify which is which and explain why."
scenario.speaker_context: Joren wants to see if Aria can separate logical validity from factual truth. A valid argument's conclusion follows necessarily from its premises, regardless of the premises' actual truth. An invalid argument allows a situation where the premises are true but the conclusion is false.

structure.pattern_description: An argument is **valid** iff there is no possible circumstance in which all premises are true while the conclusion is false. **Soundness** adds the requirement that every premise is actually true. In the example, Log Entry Alpha is valid (the conclusion follows from the two premises) but unsound because premise 2 is false – the *Sea‑Hawk* does not carry gold. Log Entry Beta is invalid because the premise does not guarantee the conclusion; a captain could command a ship once without being experienced.
structure.why_right: Recognizing validity means looking at the form of the reasoning, not the factual accuracy of the statements. Many sailors dismiss Alpha because they know the ship isn’t laden with gold, but that is a soundness judgment. Beta fails the informal test of validity: you can imagine a world where someone commands a ship once (premise true) yet remains inexperienced (conclusion false).
structure.counterpoint: A common mistake is to label an argument unsound and therefore assume it is also invalid. Validity and soundness are independent: an argument can be valid with false premises (unsound) or invalid even if all premises happen to be true.

assessment.identification_prompt: State which log entry is valid and which is invalid, and give one reason for each judgment.

rubric.description: No correct identification; provides unrelated or incorrect reasoning.
Identifies one entry correctly but confuses validity with truth of premises.
Correctly identifies both entries but gives only superficial explanations.
Correctly identifies both entries and explains the informal test of validity for each.
Provides a full answer: correct identification, clear informal‑test reasoning, and notes the soundness status of the valid argument.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Joren chuckles, "Think of a world where the premises hold but the conclusion doesn't. Can you picture such a scenario for the second entry? Try again."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Joren nods approvingly, "Well done, Captain. You’ve steered through the logic as deftly as we navigate the reefs."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff but wise; loves riddles and maritime lore.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: The sea teaches us more than just currents; it teaches us how to think. Tell me, captain, can a ship sail without a compass?
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player reaches level 4, they unlock the "Log of Clear Reasoning" item, granting a +2 bonus to future puzzle checks. If they remain at level 2 or below, Joren offers a hint and a repeat of the challenge after a short rest.

scenario.context: In the bustling guild workshop of Ironforge, Master Alaric the Dice Sage is giving a quick lesson to new apprentices about the fundamentals of probability using six‑sided dice and silver coins.
scenario.text: Master Alaric booms: "Listen up, apprentices! I have three quick challenges for you. 1) What is the probability that a fair d6 does **not** show a 4? 2) I flip two fair coins. What is the chance that at least one of them lands heads? 3) I roll a fair d6 six times in a row. What is the probability that I see at least one 4? Do NOT simply add 1/6 six times—many make that mistake and end up with 100%!
scenario.speaker_context: Alaric is emphasizing the complement rule, the corrected addition rule (accounting for overlap), and the use of negation to compute "at least one" probabilities. These concepts match the textbook axioms of non‑negativity, normalization, and the addition rule for joint events.

structure.pattern_name: Basic probability laws: complement, addition, and "at least one" via negation
structure.pattern_description: Problem 1 (complement): P(not‑4) = 1 − P(4) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. Problem 2 (addition with overlap correction): P(at least one H) = P(H₁) + P(H₂) − P(H₁∧H₂) = 1/2 + 1/2 − 1/4 = 3/4, equivalently 1 − (1/2)². Problem 3 (at least one via complement): P(at least one 4 in six rolls) = 1 − P(no 4)⁶ = 1 − (5/6)⁶ ≈ 0.665. The naïve sum 6·(1/6) = 1 is incorrect because it double‑counts overlapping outcomes.
structure.formal_form: P(¬A) = 1 − P(A).  P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∧ B).  P(at least one A in n independent trials) = 1 − [1 − P(A)]ⁿ.
structure.why_right: The complement rule turns a difficult "at least one" question into a simple "none" calculation. The addition rule must subtract the intersection to avoid double‑counting. Applying these axioms yields the exact probabilities, while the common mistake of adding raw probabilities ignores event overlap.

assessment.identification_prompt: Choose the correct probability for each of the three questions posed by Master Alaric.

rubric.description: No answer is correct or the player skips the task.
Exactly one of the three probabilities is correct.
Two of the three probabilities are correct.
All three probabilities are correct, but the reasoning provided is incomplete or contains minor errors.
All three probabilities are correct and the player accurately explains the complement and addition rules used.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Master Alaric offers a brief tutorial: "Remember, sometimes it's easier to count what *doesn't* happen. Try using the complement rule for the next attempt." The player is sent back to the dice table for a second try.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Alaric nods approvingly and awards the apprentice a "Probability Charm" that grants a small bonus to future chance‑based checks.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff yet deeply knowledgeable, Alaric loves to test apprentices with quick, bite‑size puzzles.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: A good craftsman measures twice and cuts once—so does a good mathematician count the outcomes that *don't* happen first.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correct answers unlock a new crafting recipe (Probability‑infused ink). Incorrect answers trigger a mini‑lesson module before the player may retry.

scenario.context: The player stands in the Ledger Hall of the Merchant Guild’s trading post, where merchants debate the truth of rumors about a runaway convict. An elderly logic instructor challenges the player to prove a claim using a truth table.
scenario.text: The merchant says: 'Either the convict slipped through the underground sewage tunnels (S) or he hid in the merchant's wagon (W). The convict did NOT slip through the sewage tunnels. Therefore, the convict hid in the wagon.' The instructor asks: 'Let S stand for “sewage tunnels” and W for “wagon”. Build a truth table and tell me whether this argument is valid.'
scenario.speaker_context: The instructor is a seasoned archivist who uses the classic disjunctive syllogism to teach traders how to reason about uncertain reports.

structure.pattern_name: Truth table test of validity (Disjunctive Syllogism)
structure.pattern_description: The truth‑table method checks every possible assignment of truth values to the atomic propositions. An argument is valid iff there is **no** row where all premises are true while the conclusion is false. For the argument (S ∨ W, ¬S ⟹ W) we list all four rows of S and W, evaluate the premises and the conclusion, and look for a counterexample.
structure.formal_form:
Premises: 1) S ∨ W   2) ¬S
Conclusion: W

| S | W | S ∨ W | ¬S | Premises true? | Conclusion (W) |
|---|---|-------|----|----------------|----------------|
| T | T |   T   |  F |   No (¬S false) |      T         |
| T | F |   T   |  F |   No (¬S false) |      F         |
| F | T |   T   |  T |   Yes           |      T         |
| F | F |   F   |  T |   No (S ∨ W false) |   F         |

Only the third row has both premises true, and in that row the conclusion is also true. No row makes premises true and conclusion false, so the argument is valid.
structure.why_right: The truth‑table test is exhaustive and objective: by enumerating every possible world for the atomic statements, we can see whether a counterexample exists. If none exists, the inference holds regardless of the story’s content.
structure.counterpoint: Some critics claim truth tables become unwieldy with many variables, preferring semantic tableaux or natural‑language analysis.

assessment.identification_prompt: Create the full truth table for the argument and state whether the argument is valid or invalid.

rubric.description: No attempt to construct a truth table.
Partial table with missing rows or incorrect logical operators.
Complete truth table but misidentifies the validity of the argument.
Correct truth table and correctly labels the argument as valid.
Correct table, correct validity judgment, and explains why no counterexample row exists.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Review the rows where both premises are true. Remember the argument is invalid only if you find a row with true premises and a false conclusion.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You’ve proved the argument valid. The archivist hands you a sealed ledger that may contain the convict’s hidden route.

game_hooks.npc_personality: A meticulous, slightly impatient archivist who values precision above storytelling.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: “The tunnels whisper, but the wagon rolls on. Show me the logic that ties them together.”
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player succeeds, the archivist unlocks a hidden compartment in the Ledger Hall, revealing a rare trade map that advances the main quest.

scenario.context: At a fork in the jungle trail, the player encounters Dr. Numeris, a mathematician, and Lyra, a field naturalist. Both are debating the flying ability of a mysterious bird they call "Tweets".
scenario.text: Dr. Numeris declares: "(1) Tweets is a healthy, normally functioning bird. (2) All healthy, normally functioning birds can fly. (3) Therefore, Tweets can fly." Lyra counters: "(1) Tweets is a healthy, normally functioning bird. (2) Most healthy, normally functioning birds can fly. (3) Therefore, Tweets probably can fly." She then adds, "But note—Tweets stands six feet tall and can sprint thirty miles per hour." Both turn to you. "Given this new information, whose argument still holds up?"
scenario.speaker_context: These lines are taken from a classic logic lecture that uses the 'Tweets' bird to illustrate the difference between deductive certainty and inductive probability, and how new evidence can defeat an inductive claim.

structure.pattern_name: Deductive vs inductive arguments and defeasibility
structure.pattern_description: Dr. Numeris' argument follows the classic deductive form: All F are G; x is F; therefore x is G. If the premises are true, the conclusion is guaranteed. Lyra's argument follows an inductive form: Most F are G; x is F; therefore x is probably G. Inductive conclusions are defeasible—additional premises can lower their probability. The new premise (Tweets is six feet tall and runs extremely fast) suggests a flight‑less, ostrich‑like bird, weakening Lyra's probabilistic claim while leaving the logical structure of Numeris' argument intact (though it casts doubt on premise 2).
structure.formal_form: Deductive: All F → G. x is F. ∴ x is G. (valid, not defeasible)\nInductive: Most F → G. x is F. ∴ x is probably G. (strong, but defeasible)
structure.why_right: The key distinction is that deductive arguments guarantee their conclusions if premises are true, so new evidence can only affect the truth of the premises, not the logical validity. Inductive arguments provide probable conclusions that can be weakened or overturned by additional information, as shown by the tall, fast‑running nature of Tweets.
structure.counterpoint: If later evidence showed that all six‑foot‑tall birds in this region actually possess hidden wing membranes, the inductive argument could regain strength, illustrating how defeasibility works both ways.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which type of argument (deductive or inductive) is most vulnerable to the new information about Tweets' size and speed, and why?

Names an argument type but gives an incorrect reason (e.g., says deductive is vulnerable).
Identifies the inductive argument as vulnerable but only mentions "new info" without explaining defeasibility.
Correctly identifies the inductive argument as vulnerable and notes that inductive conclusions are probabilistic and can be weakened by additional premises.

Provides a full explanation: the inductive argument is defeasible because its conclusion is only probable; the new premise (size and speed) makes a flight‑less bird more plausible, reducing the probability, whereas the deductive form remains logically valid unless a premise is shown false.

assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the insight and ask the player to rewrite Lyra's argument with a stronger premise that would restore confidence in the conclusion.

scenario.context: While patrolling the Whispering Woods, the ranger stumbles upon an old hermit who runs a hidden Symbolic Clearing. The hermit offers to teach the ranger how to translate everyday warnings into logical symbols so that the patrol can spot contradictions in enemy plans.
scenario.text: The hermit says, "Let C mean 'the campfire is lit' and I mean 'the ice bridge is safe.' Translate these two warnings into symbols: (1) The campfire will not be lit and the ice bridge will not be safe at the same time. (2) Neither the campfire will be lit nor the ice bridge will be safe tomorrow." He smiles, "These look alike, but they guide very different routes. Choose wisely!"
scenario.speaker_context: The hermit is emphasizing the distinction between negating a conjunction ('not both') and conjoining two negations ('neither‑nor'), a key skill for making sound tactical decisions.

structure.pattern_description: "Not both" is the negation of a conjunction: \(~(C \land I)\). It is true whenever at least one of the components is false – the campfire could be lit alone, the bridge could be safe alone, or both could be false. "Neither‑nor" is a conjunction of two negations: \(~C \land ~I\). It is true only when both components are false – the campfire is unlit **and** the bridge is unsafe. The two formulas are not interchangeable; the first permits one true component, the second forbids both.
structure.why_right: Correct translation respects the scope of the negation. In the first sentence the negation applies to the whole conjunction, yielding \(~(C * I)\). In the second sentence each proposition is individually negated and then conjoined, yielding \(~C * ~I\). Mixing them leads to incorrect tactical conclusions, as shown by their truth tables.
structure.counterpoint: Some learners mistakenly think that "not both" means "neither nor" because both involve negation. The counterpoint is that natural‑language phrasing often hides the logical structure; careful parsing reveals the difference.

assessment.identification_prompt: Select the correct symbolic translation for each warning:

rubric.description: Both translations are missing or completely incorrect.
One translation is correct, the other is wrong.
Both translations are present but use the wrong connectives (e.g., swapped conjunction/disjunction).
Both translations are correct but the notation is inconsistent (e.g., using "&" instead of "*" without explanation).
Both translations are correct, properly notated, and the learner can briefly explain why they differ.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The hermit chuckles, "A misplaced negation can turn a safe path into a trap. Review the difference between negating a whole statement and negating its parts, then try again."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The hermit nods approvingly, "Well done! You've earned the Insight of the Clearing. Your patrol will now spot hidden contradictions on the map."

scenario.context: Inside the bustling Grayveil Apothecary, Master Althea is guiding a new apprentice, Rowan, through the odds of selecting rare ingredients from rows of sealed jars.
scenario.text: Master Althea says: "Listen closely, Rowan. First, you reach into the shelf of six jars—one contains a mandrake root, the others hold harmless herbs. What is the probability you **do NOT** pull out the mandrake? Second, you draw two jars **with replacement** from a set that contains one golden leaf among four ordinary leaves. What is the probability that **at least one** of the draws yields the golden leaf? Finally, you will draw six times from a bin that holds five ordinary herbs and one phoenix feather. What is the probability you get **at least one** feather? Remember, you cannot simply add the single‑draw probabilities together—think about complements."
scenario.speaker_context: Master Althea is illustrating the complement rule, the addition rule with correction for overlap, and the use of complements for 'at least one' events. She emphasizes common pitfalls that novices in the apothecary trade often make.

structure.pattern_name: Basic probability laws: complement, addition, at least‑one via complement
structure.pattern_description: Problem 1 (complement): P(not‑mandrake) = 1 − P(mandrake) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. Problem 2 (addition with correction): P(at least one golden leaf) = P(golden on draw 1) + P(golden on draw 2) − P(golden on both) = 1/4 + 1/4 − 1/16 = 7/16. Equivalent complement method: 1 − (3/4)² = 7/16. Problem 3 (at least‑one via complement): P(at least one feather in 6 draws) = 1 − P(no feather)⁶ = 1 − (5/6)⁶ ≈ 0.665.
structure.formal_form: P(¬A) = 1 − P(A). P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). P(at least one A in n trials) = 1 − P(¬A)ⁿ.
structure.why_wrong: A common error is to add the single‑draw probability six times (6 × 1/6 = 1) for the third problem, which ignores the overlap of multiple successes. For the second problem, forgetting to subtract the double‑counted case (both draws golden) yields 1/2 instead of 7/16.
structure.why_right: Using the complement rule turns ‘at least one’ questions into a single‑event calculation, avoiding double‑counting. The addition rule correctly adjusts for events that can occur together, ensuring the total probability never exceeds 1.
structure.counterpoint: Rowan argues that because each draw is independent, simply summing the probabilities should work. Master Althea counters that independence does not eliminate overlap, hence the need for the subtraction term.

assessment.identification_prompt: Select the correct probability for each of Master Althea’s three questions and name the probability law you used for each.

rubric.description: Provides no answer or answers unrelated to probability.
Identifies the correct law (e.g., complement) but gives an incorrect numerical value.
Uses the correct formula but makes a minor arithmetic mistake.
Gives the correct numerical answer for each question but does not explain the reasoning.
Provides correct answers **and** clearly explains which law applies and why it is appropriate for each problem.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Master Althea smiles and says, "Think of the jars you *didn't* pick. Sometimes it's easier to count what you avoid than what you obtain. Try rewriting the problem using 1 minus the chance of the unwanted outcome."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Althea nods approvingly, "Well done! Your grasp of complements and addition will keep our potions from blowing up. Ready for a real‑world batch test?"

game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "Ah, Rowan, the mandrake whispers its odds to those who listen. What do you hear?"
game_hooks.resolution_path: Correct answers unlock a rare Nightshade leaf for the player's inventory; incorrect answers trigger a short mini‑lesson where the apprentice must repeat the three calculations with a different set of herbs before proceeding.

scenario.context: Inside the clangy heat of the Blacksmith's Forge, the master smith has etched logical formulas onto iron plates that hang above the furnace. Apprentices must determine which plates express the same truth about the metal and which do not.
scenario.text:
Master Ironhand shows three pairs of plates:

Pair 1: A → B   and   ¬A ∨ B
Pair 2: ¬(A ∧ B)   and   ¬A ∨ ¬B
Pair 3: A → B   and   B → A

He bellows: "Forge a truth table for each pair. Tell me which pairs are materially equivalent and which are not. Then explain in plain forge‑talk what each equivalence (or lack thereof) means."
scenario.speaker_context: The master blacksmith is using his craft as a metaphor for logical reasoning, drawing parallels between shaping metal and shaping arguments.

structure.pattern_name: Logical equivalence in the forge: conditionals and De Morgan's
structure.pattern_description:
Pair 1 (A → B and ¬A ∨ B) is equivalent: a conditional can be read as ‘either the antecedent is false or the consequent is true.’
Pair 2 (¬(A ∧ B) and ¬A ∨ ¬B) is equivalent: De Morgan’s Law shows that ‘not both’ equals ‘not A or not B.’
Pair 3 (A → B and B → A) is NOT equivalent: the converse of a conditional does not share the same truth conditions; a hot iron does not imply a cold hammer.
structure.formal_form: Pair 1: A→B ≡ ¬A∨B. Pair 2: ¬(A∧B) ≡ ¬A∨¬B. Pair 3: A→B ≢ B→A.
structure.why_right: Understanding equivalence lets you replace a statement with a simpler one without changing its truth. De Morgan’s Laws move negations across conjunctions and disjunctions, essential for simplifying arguments. Recognizing that a conditional and its converse are not interchangeable prevents the classic error of ‘affirming the consequent.’
structure.counterpoint: A common mistake is to think that because ‘if the metal is hot then the forge glows’ is true, the reverse ‘if the forge glows then the metal is hot’ must also be true. The exercise shows why that inference is invalid.

assessment.identification_prompt: For each pair below, indicate whether the two statements are logically equivalent (Yes) or not (No).

rubric.description: No correct identifications; explanations are absent or wholly incorrect.
Identifies one pair correctly but provides little or no justification.
Identifies two pairs correctly, with minimal explanation of why.
Identifies all three pairs correctly and explains each equivalence or non‑equivalence in plain language.
All of level 3 plus a concise formal justification (e.g., truth‑table row analysis) for each pair.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Master Ironhand hammers a new plate with the phrase “Check the fire: one ember can fool the eye.” He guides the apprentice to rebuild the truth table for the missed pair, step by step.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Satisfied, the master hands the apprentice a polished steel sigil that reads “≡”. He rewards the player with a small bonus material for the next crafting quest.

game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: He pauses his hammering, eyes the apprentice, and says, "Logic is a furnace—heat it right and the truth will melt into shape."
game_hooks.resolution_path: Upon successful completion, the player forges a ‘Logical Emblem’ that can be attached to any weapon, granting a temporary boost to strategic decision‑making in combat.

scenario.context: In the bustling forge of Ironhaven, Master Blacksmith Garrick has been producing a new line of battleaxes. Recently, a batch of axes has been reported to shatter during testing. Garrick keeps a daily log of the variables he changes while forging each batch.
scenario.text:
Garrick shows you his log:

Severe Fracture Batch 1: ore type = Meteoric (M), cooling method = water quench (W), hammer pattern = rapid (R)
Severe Fracture Batch 2: ore type = Meteoric (M), cooling method = air cool (A), hammer pattern = rapid (R)
Severe Fracture Batch 3: ore type = Meteoric (M), cooling method = water quench (W), hammer pattern = slow (S)
No‑fracture Batch 1: ore type = Iron (I), cooling method = water quench (W), hammer pattern = rapid (R)
No‑fracture Batch 2: ore type = Iron (I), cooling method = air cool (A), hammer pattern = slow (S)

Garrick asks: "Which factor is the cause of the fractures? Use the necessary‑condition test and the sufficient‑condition test."
scenario.speaker_context: The blacksmith is a seasoned craftsman who believes that understanding cause‑and‑effect will help improve his craft. The necessary‑condition test asks: which factor appears in every fracture case? The sufficient‑condition test asks: which factor never appears in a non‑fracture case.

structure.pattern_name: Mill's methods: necessary and sufficient condition tests
structure.pattern_description:
Necessary condition test: a factor X is necessary for the fracture (effect) if X is present in every fracture batch. Sufficient condition test: a factor X is sufficient for the fracture if the fracture never occurs when X is absent (equivalently, the fracture always occurs when X is present).

Applying the data:
- Ore type M appears in all three fracture batches and is absent in all non‑fracture batches → passes both tests.
- Cooling method W appears in fracture batches 1 and 3 but not batch 2 → fails the necessary test.
- Cooling method A appears in fracture batch 2 but also in a non‑fracture batch → fails the sufficient test.
- Hammer pattern R appears in fracture batches 1 and 2 but not batch 3 → fails the necessary test.
- Hammer pattern S appears in fracture batch 3 but also in a non‑fracture batch → fails the sufficient test.
Thus, the ore type Meteoric (M) is both a necessary and sufficient condition for the fractures.
structure.formal_form: Necessary condition: ∀b (Fracture(b) → X(b)). Sufficient condition: ∀b (¬X(b) → ¬Fracture(b)). Here X = "ore type is Meteoric" satisfies both.
structure.why_wrong: A common error is to pick a factor that appears frequently (e.g., water quench) but overlooks a counterexample where the factor is present without a fracture, violating the sufficient condition.
structure.why_right: Meteoric ore is the only factor that is present in every fracture batch and absent in every non‑fracture batch, satisfying both the necessary and sufficient condition tests.
structure.counterpoint: One might argue that rapid hammering contributes, but since a fracture occurred in a batch with slow hammering (Batch 3), rapid hammering cannot be the sole cause.

assessment.identification_prompt: Identify which forging variable is the cause of the axe fractures using Mill's necessary and sufficient condition tests.

rubric.description: No attempt or completely unrelated answer.
Mentions a variable but does not apply either test correctly.
Applies one of the two tests correctly but selects the wrong variable.
Applies both tests correctly but provides an incomplete justification.
Correctly identifies Meteoric ore as the cause, clearly explains why it passes both necessary and sufficient condition tests, and notes why other variables fail.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: Look for the factor that appears in *every* fracture batch and is *never* present in a batch without fractures.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! Garrick nods approvingly and asks you to source a different ore for the next batch.

game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "These axes shouldn't be splintering like dry twigs! Tell me, what in my process is making them brittle?"
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player selects Meteoric ore, the forge upgrades to a higher‑quality ore supplier, unlocking a new weapon line. If the player selects the wrong factor, Garrick offers a second chance with a hint and a minor penalty to reputation.

scenario.context: The player is summoned to the royal infirmary of Eldoria, where the court healer has just received the results of a screening test for the rare plague known as the Crimson Blight.
scenario.text: Healer Arlen says: "A noble has tested positive for Crimson Blight. The assay is 95 % accurate—it correctly flags 95 % of those who truly have the disease (sensitivity) and correctly clears 95 % of those who are healthy (specificity). The noble believes the test means there is a 95 % chance she is ill. Yet the base rate of Crimson Blight in the kingdom is only 0.5 % of the population. Compute the true probability that she is actually ill so we can advise her properly."
scenario.speaker_context: This mirrors classic base‑rate problems (e.g., taxi‑cab, medical screening). The noble is committing the base‑rate fallacy by equating test accuracy with the probability of disease given a positive result.

structure.pattern_name: Base rate reasoning in medical screening
structure.pattern_description: Assume 100 000 subjects. With a 0.5 % base rate, 500 actually have Crimson Blight. The test catches 95 % of them → 475 true positives. Of the 99 500 healthy subjects, 5 % are falsely flagged → 4 975 false positives. Total positive results = 475 + 4 975 = 5 450. Hence P(disease | positive) = 475 / 5 450 ≈ 0.087, or about 8.7 %. The noble’s true risk is roughly 9 %, not 95 %. When a condition is rare, even a highly accurate test yields many more false positives than true positives.
structure.formal_form: Base rate: P(D)=0.005. Sensitivity: P(+|D)=0.95. Specificity: P(-|¬D)=0.95 ⇒ P(+|¬D)=0.05. Population 100 000 → Diseased 500, True Pos 475, Healthy 99 500, False Pos 4 975. P(D|+)=475/(475+4 975)≈0.087.
structure.why_right: The correct answer arises from applying Bayes' theorem and explicitly accounting for the prior (base‑rate) probability of the disease. Ignoring the base rate leads to a dramatic over‑estimate of risk.
structure.counterpoint: If the disease were common (e.g., base rate 30 %), the same test would yield a much higher post‑test probability (~86 %). This contrast helps illustrate why base rates matter.

assessment.identification_prompt: What is the probability that the noble actually has Crimson Blight given a positive test result?

rubric.description: No attempt or answer unrelated to probability.
Provides a numeric answer but does not show any reasoning or uses only test accuracy (e.g., 95 %).
Mentions the need for base rates but gives an incorrect calculation (e.g., 5 % or 50 %).
Correctly sets up the Bayes calculation but makes a minor arithmetic error (result ≈ 9 % instead of 8.7 %).
Accurately computes the probability (~8.7 %) and explains why the base rate dramatically lowers the risk despite high test accuracy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The healer gently explains: "Think of a crowd of 100 000 people. Only a few have the plague, but the false‑positive rate applies to everyone else. Let’s count the true and false positives together to see the true risk."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Arlen smiles and says: "Well done! Now we can tell the noble that her chance of illness is low, and we can focus on monitoring rather than panic."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Healer Arlen is methodical, patient, and enjoys teaching the party about logic and medicine.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: ‘The numbers speak louder than fear. Let me show you how…’
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player computes the correct probability, the noble is reassured and grants the party a modest reward of healing herbs. If they err, the noble insists on a costly, unnecessary isolation, and the party must spend extra resources to rectify the mistake.

scenario.text: Dr. Lira addresses the rookie medics: "Listen up! I have three quick problems. First, a sealed medical kit contains 6 identical bandage packs, one of which is contaminated. If we randomly pull a pack, what is the probability it is NOT contaminated? Second, we have two independent blood‑type tests, each with a 50% chance of a false positive. What is the probability that at least one test reports a false positive? Third, we will draw a bandage pack six times with replacement. What is the probability that we see at least one contaminated pack? Remember: don't just add the single‑draw probabilities together—use the right rules!"
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Lira is explicitly teaching the complement rule (P(not A)=1‑P(A)), the addition rule with overlap correction (P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)‑P(A∧B)), and the use of complement for "at least one" events. These map directly to the A4.1 learning objectives.

structure.pattern_name: Basic probability laws: complement, addition, and "at least one" via complement
structure.pattern_description: Problem 1 (complement): P(not‑contaminated)=1‑P(contaminated)=1‑1/6=5/6. Problem 2 (addition with correction): P(at least one false positive)=P(FP₁)+P(FP₂)‑P(both FP)=½+½‑¼=¾. Equivalently, use complement: 1‑P(no false positives)=1‑(½)²=¾. Problem 3 ("at least one" via complement): P(at least one contaminated in 6 draws)=1‑P(no contaminated)⁶=1‑(5/6)⁶≈0.665. The naïve sum 6×1/6=1 is a classic error that the complement rule avoids.
structure.formal_form: P(¬A)=1‑P(A)\nP(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)‑P(A∧B)\nP(at least one A in n trials)=1‑[P(¬A)]ⁿ
structure.why_right: The complement rule turns a difficult "at least one" calculation into a simple "none" calculation. The addition rule prevents double‑counting when two events can occur together. Mastering these tools lets medics quickly evaluate risk under pressure, exactly as the battlefield scenario demands.
structure.counterpoint: A common misconception is to think that because each draw has a 1/6 chance of contamination, six draws must guarantee a contaminated pack (6×1/6=1). This ignores the possibility of repeated non‑contaminated draws.

scenario.speaker_context: Cassian is a charismatic but overconfident actor who loves to blend theatrical flair with half‑baked logic. He assumes that a property of every component of his costume automatically applies to the whole performer.

The emergent property of visibility depends on the collective structure, not merely on the parts.
structure.counterpoint: The inference would be valid for properties that are strictly additive, such as material composition: if every part of a statue is bronze, the statue is bronze. Visibility, however, is not additive; it emerges from how parts interact with light.

scenario.context: At the bustling Larkhaven trading post, merchant Alric discovers that his sealed barrel of rare saffron has vanished from the storage cellar overnight.
scenario.text: Alric confronts the night watchman, Garret. "If thieves stole the saffron, they'd have to break the wax seal on the barrel. Look, the seal is shattered. So thieves must have taken it. I'll have you raise the alarm and gather a militia!"
scenario.speaker_context: Garret is diligent but jumps to conclusions. Broken seals could also result from a careless apprentice, a stray animal, or a faulty seal that cracked on its own.

structure.pattern_description: Garret reasons from "If thieves stole the saffron then the seal would be broken" and "the seal is broken" to conclude "thieves stole the saffron." He treats the consequent as sufficient proof of the antecedent.
structure.formal_form: If P then Q. Q. Therefore P.
structure.why_wrong: The conditional tells us that a theft would cause a broken seal, but a broken seal can arise from many other causes. Observing a broken seal does not guarantee a theft occurred.
structure.counterpoint: The reasoning would only be valid if the conditional were reversed: "If the seal is broken, then thieves stole the saffron," which would require that broken seals can only result from theft.

assessment.identification_prompt: Garret is convinced thieves took the saffron because the seal is broken. Does his conclusion logically follow from the evidence?

rubric.description: Agrees with Garret that thieves must be responsible.
Expresses doubt about Garret's certainty but cannot explain the reasoning flaw.

scenario.context: In the sleepy fishing village of Gullhaven, the communal net‑storage hut was found empty at first light. The wooden door was still latched, and no footprints or broken locks were discovered on the sand‑washed floor. Three villagers each put forward a different explanation for the missing nets.
scenario.text:
Mira the fisherwoman says: "A storm spirit must have swept the nets into the sea while we slept. The wind was fierce last night, and the spirit is known to take what the villagers hoard. That would explain why nothing looks forced."

Tor the dockmaster says: "Old Joren, the night watch, slipped the nets out through the back hatch and sold them to a rival port. He has the only key, his ledger shows overdue debts, and the fresh rope marks on the dock match the path to the hidden cove where smugglers hide."

Lysa the herbalist says: "The wandering mage from the cliffs stole the nets to use the fibers in a powerful binding spell. He can vanish without leaving a trace, which is why the door is untouched."
scenario.speaker_context: The player, acting as the village elder, must evaluate which of the three explanations best accounts for the evidence using the seven explanatory virtues of IBE: testability, scope, simplicity, mechanism, fruitfulness, consistency with background knowledge, and explanatory power.

structure.pattern_name: Inference to the best explanation and explanatory virtues
structure.pattern_description: IBE selects the hypothesis that most powerfully accounts for the observed facts while satisfying the explanatory virtues. Mira's spirit hypothesis introduces a supernatural entity that cannot be tested and conflicts with the village's known naturalistic worldview, failing on simplicity, testability, and consistency. Lysa's mage hypothesis likewise adds an unverified magical actor, offering no mechanism and lacking fruitfulness. Tor's watchman‑theft hypothesis is parsimonious, testable (inspect Joren's accounts, interview dock workers, examine the rope marks), and explains all observed evidence: no forced entry, the presence of a key holder, motive, and physical traces. Therefore Tor's explanation scores highest on simplicity, testability, and explanatory power, making it the best explanation.
structure.why_wrong: Mira's and Lysa's hypotheses rely on unobservable supernatural agents, violate the virtue of simplicity, and cannot be falsified, so they are inferior explanations.
structure.why_right: Tor's hypothesis is simple, testable, offers a clear mechanism, aligns with known background facts about Joren's debts, and explains all evidence, satisfying the majority of the explanatory virtues.
structure.counterpoint: In some cases multiple hypotheses may share virtues; the player should weigh which virtues are most critical for the specific context.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which villager's explanation provides the best overall account of the missing nets according to the explanatory virtues of IBE?

rubric.description: Provides no justification or selects randomly.
Names a virtue but does not connect it to any hypothesis.
Mentions one or two virtues and selects a hypothesis, but the connection is weak or partially incorrect.
Correctly selects Tor's hypothesis and justifies it using at least three explanatory virtues (e.g., simplicity, testability, explanatory power).
Offers a thorough comparative analysis of all three hypotheses, ranks them, and explains the choice using all seven virtues, showing deep understanding of IBE.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider which explanation can be investigated with evidence you have on hand. Ask yourself: which hypothesis introduces the fewest new entities and can be checked in the village?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Excellent! Your reasoning aligns with the principles of IBE. The watchman's theft is uncovered, and the village can now retrieve the nets and address Joren's debts.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mira is hopeful and superstitious, Tor is pragmatic and skeptical, Lysa is curious and secretive.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Mira: "The sea whispers of spirits..." Tor: "I've seen Joren's ledgers; they're not a joke." Lysa: "Magic is rarely seen, but it moves in shadows."
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player selects Tor's explanation, they receive a clue to inspect Joren's key and discover a hidden ledger, leading to a side quest to confront Joren and recover the nets. Choosing the wrong explanation triggers a minor penalty and a hint to re‑evaluate the virtues.

scenario.context: In the bustling Sunfire Marketplace, the player overhears a debate between two stall owners about the value of their wares. The conversation takes place near a row of items ranging from a simple wooden spoon to an intricately crafted silver chalice.
scenario.text: "Look at this line of goods," Merchant Corin says, gesturing from the cheap wooden spoon to the glittering chalice. "Can you point out exactly where a 'cheap' item becomes a 'expensive' one? There’s no sharp line—each piece is just a tiny step up in price. If we can’t draw a precise boundary, then the whole distinction between cheap and expensive is meaningless. All these items are essentially the same in value; the price tags are just arbitrary nonsense!"
scenario.speaker_context: Corin is a shrewd but overly pedantic merchant who uses the absence of a clear price boundary to argue that no real price distinctions exist. He is employing a conceptual slippery‑slope (sorites) fallacy, conflating vagueness with equivalence.

structure.pattern_description: Corin exploits the gradual nature of price differences. Because there is no single, sharp point where a good switches from 'cheap' to 'expensive', he concludes that the categories themselves are meaningless, denying any real distinction between low‑ and high‑value items.
structure.formal_form: There is no sharp boundary between cheap and moderately priced. There is no sharp boundary between moderately priced and expensive. ... Therefore there is no real difference between cheap and expensive.
structure.why_wrong: The inability to pinpoint an exact moment where a price jumps from cheap to expensive does not eliminate the substantive difference between the extremes. A wooden spoon and a silver chalice differ enormously in material, craftsmanship, and utility, even if price increases incrementally. Vagueness in categorisation does not erase real economic distinctions.
structure.counterpoint: If Corin’s argument were sound, we would have to treat a pebble and a diamond as having the same worth, which contradicts everyday experience and market practice.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which logical fallacy is Merchant Corin committing in his argument about price categories?

rubric.description: No attempt to name a fallacy or an unrelated answer.
Mentions a fallacy but selects one that does not fit (e.g., straw man).
Correctly identifies the fallacy as a "conceptual slippery slope" or "sorites fallacy".
Identifies the fallacy and explains why the gradual price change does not eliminate real differences.
Provides a clear identification, a solid explanation, and offers a concise counter‑argument that could be used in‑game.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: Think about how the argument moves from "no sharp line" to "all items are the same". What kind of reasoning links vague boundaries to a claim that the categories are meaningless?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You spotted the conceptual slippery‑slope fallacy. Use this insight to challenge Corin’s pricing logic.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Corin is meticulous about numbers, loves to sound philosophical, and often tries to convince customers that price tags are arbitrary.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Ask Corin to justify why a wooden spoon and a silver chalice should be treated the same, then point out concrete differences in material and function.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can present a series of contrasting examples (e.g., a cracked mug vs. a flawless crystal goblet) to demonstrate clear value gaps, prompting Corin to concede a modest discount on the chalice.

scenario.context: During the grand tournament, the champion's tent is bustling with spectators. A charismatic alchemist named Mirra Mirth has set up a small stall offering a 'Victory Tonic' that promises to restore an athlete's peak performance after a slump.
scenario.text: Mirra lifts a gleaming vial filled with a swirling amber liquid. 'Just two days ago, Sir Alden the Archer missed every shot in the archery challenge. He felt his confidence crumble, his hands shook, and the crowd laughed. He drank a single dose of my Victory Tonic, and look at him now—hitting bullseyes like never before! Ten out of ten athletes who tried my tonic felt stronger within 48 hours. Who else can claim such results?'
scenario.speaker_context: Mirra is capitalizing on the fact that athletes often perform poorly when they are at a low point, and naturally tend to improve as they recover confidence or as fatigue fades. This natural rebound—regression to the mean—is being presented as evidence of the tonic's efficacy.

structure.pattern_description: An extreme negative observation (poor performance) is followed by a return toward typical performance levels. The improvement is incorrectly attributed to an intervention (the tonic) when the more parsimonious explanation is natural recovery toward the mean.
structure.why_wrong: Performance slumps are often temporary; athletes usually bounce back as fatigue dissipates or confidence rebuilds. By promoting the tonic at the moment of the slump, Mirra makes it appear causal, but the same rebound would likely have occurred without any potion. Proper evidence would require a control group of equally slumped athletes who did not receive the tonic.
structure.counterpoint: Not every improvement after a low point is due to regression; some interventions genuinely help. The key is to distinguish natural rebound from true causal effects through controlled comparison.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mirra exploiting when she claims her Victory Tonic causes athletes to recover quickly after a poor performance?

rubric.description: No identification of the bias; response unrelated.
Mentions a bias but incorrectly names it (e.g., "confirmation bias").
Identifies the correct bias (regression to the mean) but provides an incomplete or inaccurate explanation.
Correctly identifies regression to the mean and gives a clear, mostly accurate explanation of why the tonic’s claim is flawed.
Fully identifies regression to the mean, explains the reasoning with concrete examples, and suggests how a proper test could be designed.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Explain that athletes often improve naturally after a slump because extreme performance tends to move back toward average. Ask the player to think of a way to test the tonic’s effect without the bias.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Praise the insight and challenge the player to design a simple experiment (e.g., a control group) that could verify whether the tonic truly works.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Flamboyant showman who loves grand gestures, persuasive language, and dramatic flair.

game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (1) accept the tonic and later notice the lack of effect, (2) challenge Mirra to a public demonstration with a control group, or (3) ignore the pitch and continue the tournament, gaining a reputation for critical thinking.

scenario.context: Inside the heated Proof Forge, the apprentice blacksmith‑scholar stands before a massive iron slab etched with logical symbols. The master instructor, a grizzled smith named Ferron, gestures to the chalk‑covered surface.
scenario.text: Ferron writes: "Given the premises (1) A → B, (2) C → D, (3) A ∨ C. Derive the conclusion B ∨ D. You may use any of the eight natural‑deduction rules. Think both forwards from what you have and backwards from what you need. Which rule can create a disjunction like our target? Which premises can you combine right now?"
scenario.speaker_context: Ferron is urging the player to practice the backward‑forward strategy: identify a rule that yields a disjunction (the conclusion) and then see which premises fit that rule.

structure.pattern_description: The proof hinges on the constructive dilemma rule: from a disjunction P ∨ Q together with conditionals P → R and Q → S, one may infer R ∨ S. Working backwards, the conclusion B ∨ D is a disjunction, suggesting constructive dilemma. Working forwards, the premises provide exactly the required shape (A ∨ C, A → B, C → D). Applying constructive dilemma yields B ∨ D in a single step.
structure.formal_form:
1. A → B          premise
2. C → D          premise
3. A ∨ C          premise
4. B ∨ D          constructive dilemma 1,2,3
structure.why_right: The backward scan spots the disjunction in the goal and points to rules that introduce disjunctions. Constructive dilemma is the only rule that simultaneously uses a disjunction and two conditionals, matching the three available premises. The forward scan confirms that the premises fit the rule, allowing the proof to close in one move. This dual‑direction reasoning exemplifies strategic natural‑deduction problem solving.
structure.counterpoint: Alternative proofs exist: one could assume A, derive B via Modus Ponens, then discharge the assumption to get A → B, repeat for C → D, and finally use disjunction introduction twice. These routes are longer and illustrate that multiple valid strategies can reach the same conclusion.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which natural‑deduction rule should you apply to obtain the disjunction B ∨ D from the given premises?

rubric.description: Student cannot name any applicable rule or provides an unrelated rule.
Student mentions a rule that produces a disjunction (e.g., Disjunction Introduction) but does not explain why it fits the premises.
Student correctly identifies Constructive Dilemma but cannot justify the selection of the three premises.
Student names Constructive Dilemma and correctly links each premise to the required components (A ∨ C, A → B, C → D).
Student not only selects Constructive Dilemma with full justification but also writes the complete one‑step derivation and explains the backward‑forward reasoning strategy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Ferron nods sympathetically and says, "Think about how a disjunction appears in a conclusion. Which rule actually *creates* a new disjunction rather than just adding one? Then check which of your premises match the pattern of that rule."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Ferron smiles, "Exactly! The constructive dilemma fuses the disjunction with the two conditionals. You’ve forged the proof in a single strike. Let’s see if you can apply the same tactic to a more tangled set of premises."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff but encouraging master blacksmith, loves analogies between metalwork and logic.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "A good blade, like a good proof, is forged by heating the metal of premises and striking with the right hammer of inference. What hammer will you wield for this disjunction?"
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player selects Constructive Dilemma and writes the one‑step proof, the forge glows brighter and the iron slab cracks open, revealing the next chamber. If the player chooses a longer route, the forge still opens but with a delayed timer, prompting a reflection on efficiency.

scenario.context: Inside the war room of Castle Blackstone, the siege commander has laid out three enchanted banners. Each banner bears a pair of logical statements that the player must evaluate before the next assault can be launched.
scenario.text:
The commander points to the banners and says: "We must know which of these statements are truly the same, for only equivalent tactics will hold under any circumstance.

Banner 1: 𝑆 → 𝑇   and   ¬𝑆 ∨ 𝑇.
Banner 2:   ¬(𝑆 ∧ 𝑈)   and   ¬𝑆 ∨ ¬𝑈.
Banner 3:   𝑆 → 𝑇   and   𝑇 → 𝑆.

Build truth tables for each pair, tell me which pairs are logically equivalent and which are not, and explain in plain language what the equivalence (or lack thereof) means for our siege plans."
scenario.speaker_context: The commander is teaching the troops how to spot logical equivalence, using the conditional-as-disjunction rule, De Morgan's Laws, and the non‑equivalence of a conditional with its converse.

structure.pattern_name: Logical equivalence: conditional-as-disjunction, De Morgan, and converse
structure.pattern_description: Banner 1 shows the classic equivalence of a conditional and a disjunction (𝑆 → 𝑇 ≡ ¬𝑆 ∨ 𝑇). Banner 2 illustrates De Morgan's Law (¬(𝑆 ∧ 𝑈) ≡ ¬𝑆 ∨ ¬𝑈). Banner 3 demonstrates that a conditional is **not** equivalent to its converse (𝑆 → 𝑇 ↛ 𝑇 → 𝑆).
structure.formal_form: Banner 1: 𝑆→𝑇 ⇔ ¬𝑆 ∨ 𝑇.\nBanner 2: ¬(𝑆∧𝑈) ⇔ ¬𝑆 ∨ ¬𝑈.\nBanner 3: 𝑆→𝑇 ≠ 𝑇→𝑆 (counterexample: 𝑆=T, 𝑇=F).
structure.why_right: Recognizing logical equivalence lets commanders replace complex conditions with simpler, equivalent ones, avoiding misinterpretation of orders. De Morgan's Law is essential when negating combined conditions (e.g., "the drawbridge is not both raised and locked"). Knowing that a conditional and its converse are not interchangeable prevents the common mistake of assuming "if the battering ram breaks the gate, the defenders will flee" also means "if the defenders flee, the battering ram will break the gate."
structure.counterpoint: A common misconception is to treat the converse of a conditional as automatically true; this pattern explicitly shows why that belief is false.

assessment.identification_prompt: For each banner, state whether the two statements are logically equivalent. If they are, write the equivalence symbol (≡); if not, write “not equivalent”. Then give a one‑sentence plain‑language explanation.

rubric.description: Provides no answer or answers unrelated to logical equivalence.
Identifies equivalence status for at most one banner, with little or no explanation.
Correctly identifies equivalence for two banners, but explanation is vague or partially incorrect.
Correctly identifies equivalence for all three banners and gives clear, accurate explanations for each.
All of level 3 plus demonstrates reasoning by constructing a truth table or citing a counterexample for the non‑equivalent pair.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The commander points to the banner in question and says, "Let's build the truth table together. See how the rows differ? Try again with that insight."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The commander nods approvingly, "Well done! Use these equivalences to rewrite the siege orders so they are unambiguous under any battlefield condition."

scenario.context: In the quiet scriptorium of Saint Aldric's monastery, Brother Tomas, the resident healer, has just received the result of a new diagnostic test for Grey Rot, a disease that afflicts only 1% of the local population.
scenario.text: Brother Tomas peers at the parchment bearing the test result and exclaims, "The test is 90% accurate and it came back positive for Grey Rot. That means there is a 90% chance this pilgrim is infected! We must begin the harsh purgative regimen at once. Time is of the essence!" He rushes to gather the bitter herbs and tinctures.
scenario.speaker_context: Brother Tomas is a diligent healer who has mistakenly equated the test's accuracy with the individual's probability of disease, completely overlooking the low base rate of Grey Rot.

structure.pattern_description: Brother Tomas assumes that a positive result on a 90% accurate test translates to a 90% chance of disease, ignoring that Grey Rot only occurs in 1% of the population. For a cohort of 10,000 people: 100 actually have Grey Rot. The test correctly identifies 90 of them (true positives). Among the 9,900 healthy individuals, 5% will be false‑positive = 495. Total positives = 90 + 495 = 585. Thus the true probability of disease given a positive test is 90 / 585 ≈ 15.4%.
structure.formal_form: P(D|+) = \frac{P(+|D) \times P(D)}{P(+|D) \times P(D) + P(+|\neg D) \times P(\neg D)} = \frac{0.90 \times 0.01}{0.90 \times 0.01 + 0.10 \times 0.99} \approx 0.154.
structure.why_wrong: When a condition is rare, even a test with high sensitivity and specificity yields many more false positives than true positives. The 90% accuracy describes the test's performance, not the chance that this specific pilgrim is sick. Ignoring the base rate inflates the perceived risk from ~15% to an erroneous 90%.
structure.counterpoint: Encourage the player to calculate the posterior probability using Bayes' theorem and to suggest waiting for a confirmatory test before initiating treatment.

scenario.context: The traveling theater troupe "The Silver Lantern" has been performing a new comedy across several villages. After each performance, the troupe records which production elements were present on nights when the audience laughed loudly versus nights when the audience was silent.
scenario.text:
Performance Log:

Laugh Night 1: bright lighting (L), live orchestra (O), improvisational jokes (J).
Laugh Night 2: bright lighting (L), no orchestra, improvisational jokes (J).
Laugh Night 3: bright lighting (L), live orchestra (O), scripted jokes (S).
Silent Night 1: dim lighting, live orchestra (O), scripted jokes (S).
Silent Night 2: dim lighting, no orchestra, improvisational jokes (J).

The director asks the player: "Which element caused the audience to laugh? Use the necessary‑condition test and the sufficient‑condition test."
scenario.speaker_context: The director explains that the necessary‑condition test asks: which element appears in every laughing night? The sufficient‑condition test asks: which element never appears on a silent night? The player must apply Mill’s methods of agreement and difference to pinpoint the causal factor.

structure.pattern_name: Mill's methods: necessary and sufficient condition tests
structure.pattern_description:
Necessary‑condition test: an element X is necessary for the effect E if X is present whenever E occurs. Sufficient‑condition test: an element X is sufficient for E if E never occurs when X is absent (equivalently, E always occurs when X is present). Applying the data:
- Bright lighting (L) appears on all three laughing nights and on no silent night → passes both tests.
- Live orchestra (O) appears on Laugh Night 1 and 3 but is absent on Laugh Night 2, so it fails the necessary test.
- Improvisational jokes (J) appear on Laugh Night 1 and 2 but are missing on Laugh Night 3, so they fail the necessary test.
- Scripted jokes (S) never appear on laughing nights, so they fail both tests.
Thus, bright lighting (L) is identified as the cause of audience laughter.
structure.formal_form:
Necessary condition: ∀e (E(e) → X(e)).
Sufficient condition: ∀e (¬X(e) → ¬E(e)).
Data shows L satisfies both.
structure.why_wrong: A common mistake is to claim the live orchestra (O) is the cause because it appears on two laughing nights. This ignores Laugh Night 2, where laughter occurred without O, violating the necessary‑condition test.
structure.why_right: Bright lighting (L) is present on every laughing night and absent on every silent night, meeting both the necessary and sufficient criteria, making it the correct causal factor.
structure.counterpoint: If the troupe had additional data showing a night with bright lighting but a silent audience, L would fail the sufficient test, prompting a re‑evaluation of the causal claim.

assessment.identification_prompt: Using the logs, state which production element caused the audience to laugh and justify your answer with the necessary‑condition and sufficient‑condition tests.

rubric.description: No answer or answer unrelated to the logs.
Identifies an element but provides no reasoning or uses only one test incorrectly.
Identifies an element and mentions one of the two tests correctly, but the other test is missing or flawed.
Correctly identifies bright lighting (L) and applies both tests, but explanation contains minor logical slips.
Accurately identifies bright lighting (L) and clearly demonstrates both necessary‑condition and sufficient‑condition reasoning with no errors.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Review the definition of a necessary condition: it must appear in every laughing night. Which element satisfies that? Then check which element never appears on a silent night for the sufficient condition.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You've correctly used Mill's methods to isolate the cause. The troupe will now ensure bright lighting for every performance.

game_hooks.npc_personality: The meticulous stage manager, always obsessed with lighting cues and sound balance.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: "We need to know why the crowd is quiet. Look at the logs—what repeats when they laugh? What never shows up when they’re silent?"
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player selects bright lighting, the stage manager nods approvingly and upgrades the troupe's lighting rig. If the player selects a wrong element, the manager points out the inconsistency and offers a hint about the necessary‑condition test.

scenario.context: In the quiet scriptorium of Saint Verena's Monastery, novice monk Brother Anselm is leading a midday discussion on the nature of perception. He wants to impress the senior monks with a clever argument about the visibility of the cloister.
scenario.text: "Listen, brothers! Every single stone that makes up our cloister is too small to be seen individually without a magnifying glass. Since the cloister is composed only of those stones, the whole cloister must be invisible to the naked eye!" He gestures toward the vaulted arches, claiming they disappear before his eyes.
scenario.speaker_context: Brother Anselm is a eager novice who has just learned about logical fallacies but confuses the direction of the argument. He assumes that a property of each part (being too small to see) automatically applies to the assembled whole.

structure.pattern_description: An argument that a property true of each component of a whole must also be true of the whole itself, without checking whether the property actually aggregates.
structure.formal_form: ∀x (x ∈ parts_of X → P(x)) ⇒ P(X)
structure.why_wrong: Visibility is not a property that necessarily transfers from parts to the whole. While individual stones may be too small to see alone, their arrangement into a wall creates a structure that is readily visible. The fallacy ignores emergent properties that arise from the combination of parts.
structure.counterpoint: The inference would be valid for properties that are purely compositional, such as material composition: if every part of a statue is bronze, the statue is bronze. For perceptual properties like visibility, the whole can behave very differently from its parts.

assessment.identification_prompt: Brother Anselm is confident in his proof that the cloister is invisible. Is his reasoning sound? Identify the flaw.

rubric.description: No recognition of any error; repeats Anselm's claim.
Notes something is off but cannot name the specific fallacy.
Identifies that the argument confuses parts with the whole, but does not label it.
Correctly names the composition fallacy and explains why visibility does not transfer from parts to whole.
Provides a clear, concise explanation, gives a correct counter‑example, and suggests how to reformulate the argument properly.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The senior monk steps in: "Anselm, consider a tapestry made of countless threads. Each thread is thin, yet the tapestry is a vivid picture. Some properties change when parts combine. Think about why visibility might be one of those properties."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The abbot smiles: "Well reasoned! You have uncovered the composition error. Let us use this insight when we study other teachings, such as the difference between individual virtues and the virtue of a community."

scenario.context: In the Whispering Canyon bandit hideout, the leader, Mara the Sharp, has noticed that the alarm bells go off on certain nights, alerting rival patrols. She has kept a log of three factors that might influence the alarms: moonlight intensity (M), guard shift change time (G), and a recent supply drop (S). The player is asked to help Mara apply Mill's methods to pinpoint the cause of the alarms.
scenario.text:
Mara shows the log:

Alarm Night 1: bright moon (M), guard shift at 22:00 (G), supply drop today (S).
Alarm Night 2: bright moon (M), guard shift at 22:00 (G), no supply drop.
Alarm Night 3: dim moon (no M), guard shift at 22:00 (G), supply drop today (S).
No‑alarm Night 1: dim moon (no M), guard shift at 20:00 (no G), no supply drop.
No‑alarm Night 2: bright moon (M), guard shift at 20:00 (no G), no supply drop.

Mara asks: "Which factor is the cause of the alarms? Use the necessary‑condition test and the sufficient‑condition test."
scenario.speaker_context: The bandit leader is explicitly teaching the player how to use Mill's agreement and difference methods. The necessary‑condition test asks: which factor appears in every alarm night? The sufficient‑condition test asks: which factor never appears on a night without an alarm?

structure.pattern_name: Mill's methods: necessary and sufficient condition tests
structure.pattern_description:
Necessary‑condition test: Identify the factor that is present in all alarm nights. Factor G (guard shift at 22:00) appears on all three alarm nights, while M is missing on night 3 and S is missing on night 2. Therefore G passes the necessary‑condition test. 
Sufficient‑condition test: Identify the factor that is absent on every no‑alarm night. G is absent on both no‑alarm nights (shift at 20:00), while M appears on no‑alarm night 2 and S appears on none. Since the alarm never occurs without G, G also passes the sufficient‑condition test. Thus G (the 22:00 guard shift) is both necessary and sufficient for the alarm.
structure.formal_form: Necessary condition: X is necessary for E if ∀ cases (E ⇒ X). Sufficient condition: X is sufficient for E if ∀ cases (X ⇒ E). Here, G satisfies both ∀(Alarm ⇒ G) and ∀(¬G ⇒ ¬Alarm).
structure.why_wrong: If a player selects M or S, they miss that those factors are not present on every alarm night (M missing on night 3, S missing on night 2) and they appear on at least one no‑alarm night (M on no‑alarm night 2).
structure.why_right: Choosing G is correct because the 22:00 guard shift occurs every time the alarm sounds and never occurs on a night without the alarm, satisfying both the necessary‑condition and sufficient‑condition criteria.
structure.counterpoint: One could argue that a combination of factors (e.g., bright moon + guard shift) might be required, but the data already shows the guard shift alone perfectly predicts the alarm, making it the simplest sufficient cause.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which single factor is the cause of the alarm bells according to Mill's necessary‑ and sufficient‑condition tests?

rubric.description: Provides no answer or an unrelated statement.
Names a factor but cannot justify it with the tests.
Identifies a factor and mentions one of the two tests correctly.
Correctly identifies the guard shift (G) and explains both the necessary‑condition and sufficient‑condition reasoning, but with minor logical gaps.
Accurately selects G, fully articulates why it satisfies both tests, and contrasts it with the incorrect factors, showing deep understanding of Mill's methods.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Mara sighs, "The moon and supplies are tempting clues, but look again at the nights without alarms. What never appears there?" The player is guided to re‑examine the guard shift column.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Mara nods approvingly, "Exactly. The 22:00 shift triggers the alarm. Now, can you devise a plan to change the shift and avoid detection?" The player gains a bonus to the next stealth check.

scenario.context: The party has tracked the Red Fang bandits to their hidden cavern deep in the Whispering Woods. Inside, they confront the bandit captain, Krel, who is debating whether to allow a lone merchant to trade for supplies.
scenario.text: "If we let that merchant slip into our hideout, he'll see our caches. Word will spread, more townsfolk will demand a share. To keep them quiet we'll have to lower our guard. Lower guard means a rival gang will attack. That attack will force us into a blood‑soaked war, and the whole forest will be razed. One small trade is the first step toward the destruction of our refuge!"
scenario.speaker_context: Krel is the self‑appointed leader of the Red Fang bandits. He fears losing control of the hideout and exaggerates the consequences of a single trade to maintain his authority.

structure.pattern_description: Krel strings together a chain of causal claims—allowing a merchant leads to exposure, exposure leads to demands, demands lead to lowered guard, lowered guard leads to rival attack, rival attack leads to war, war leads to forest destruction—treating each link as inevitable without evidence.
structure.formal_form: A → B. B → C. C → D. … Therefore A → Z. (But P(B|A)·P(C|B)·…·P(Z|Y) is far less than 1.)
structure.why_wrong: Each step in the chain has its own probability. Multiplying several less‑than‑certain probabilities yields a much smaller overall chance, so the conclusion that A guarantees Z is unjustified. The argument confuses plausibility of individual links with certainty of the whole sequence.
structure.counterpoint: If any link in the chain were truly near‑certain (backed by solid evidence), the chain could be persuasive. In Krel's case, none of the steps are proven, making the whole claim speculative.

Correctly identifies the fallacy as a slippery‑slope but provides no justification.
Identifies the slippery‑slope and explains why the chain of causation is unjustified.
Identifies the slippery‑slope, explains the probabilistic error, and proposes a concrete counterargument that breaks the chain.
